grounds.point: Section 14(1)(b) requires qualifying subletting, assignment or parting with possession without the landlord's written consent.
grounds.explanation: The supplied Delhi provisions make subletting, assignment or other parting with possession after the specified date actionable when the required written consent has not been obtained, and section 16 likewise requires previous written consent for post-Act subletting or transfer.

grounds.point: M/s Anil & Co. Pvt. Ltd. has carried on business from the suit premises since 1997.
grounds.explanation: The respondent's own pleaded case states that its partners were carrying on business as directors of M/s Anil & Co. Pvt. Ltd. from the suit property since 1997, and the petitioner's submissions rely on corresponding admissions. Operation of another corporate entity from the premises is relevant, but section 14(1)(b) still requires a qualifying subletting, assignment or parting with possession.

grounds.point: Dhian Nath Kapur and Mrs. Anil Kapur were both partners of the respondent firm and directors of M/s Anil & Co. Pvt. Ltd.
grounds.explanation: The respondent pleaded this overlap, and its documentary evidence included a bank certificate identifying the same two persons as directors since 1997. This evidence supports the respondent's opposition to an inference that occupation by the company necessarily displaced the tenant's own possession, but the supplied record contains no target-court finding resolving actual possession or control.

grounds.point: The respondent transferred exclusive possession or control of the suit premises to M/s Anil & Co. Pvt. Ltd.
grounds.explanation: The petitioner argued that operation by the company established or permitted an inference of subletting, while the respondent maintained that the same partners continued the business and retained possession. The supplied Delhi provision and reported Parasaram discussion show that section 14(1)(b) extends broadly to assignment or other modes of parting with possession, including involuntary transfer, but the allowed record provides no preserved finding that possession or control was actually parted with on these facts.

grounds.point: The landlord gave the written consent required for the alleged post-1952 transfer or occupation.
grounds.explanation: The respondent alleged that the original landlord permitted Kapur family members to carry on business and relied on a 1964 rent receipt and later landlord intimation, but the supplied descriptions do not establish that either document contains written consent to the particular subletting, assignment or parting with possession alleged here. Because absence of supplied proof of written consent is not itself proof that no written consent existed, this statutory condition remains unresolved on the allowed record.

grounds.point: The succession of the tenancy through Dina Nath Kapur's Will independently constitutes actionable parting with possession under the supplied Delhi law.
grounds.explanation: The respondent acknowledged succession through a Will, while the petitioner submitted that testamentary vesting amounted to parting with possession and the respondent asserted landlord agreement. The supplied original Delhi material establishes the broad reach of section 14(1)(b) but does not supply a controlling rule resolving testamentary succession in these particular circumstances or the effect of the asserted landlord agreement, so this proposed independent route to eviction cannot be determined from the permitted law.

reason: The allowed material establishes third-party corporate business activity and supplies a broad statutory prohibition, but it does not resolve whether the tenant actually parted with possession or whether the required written consent existed. The separate Will-based theory also exceeds what the supplied original Delhi authorities conclusively resolve, so the fixed section 14(1)(b) ground remains undetermined.
